Carport calculator

Timber and cost for a flat-roof carport. Length and width are the outside size of the roof, including a 30 cm overhang.

How the carport is built

The calculator assumes the classic design: two rows of posts each carry a beam, and the rafters sit across the beams. Knee braces between posts and beams stiffen the frame along its length. The beams overhang 30 cm at both ends, and the rafters 30 cm on each side.

The number of posts follows from the maximum post spacing. The further apart the posts, the deeper the beam has to be. The rafters are spaced at about 700 mm centres, and their size depends on the span between the beams.

Which timber is best for a carport?

C24 structural softwood is kiln dried, stable and the cheapest choice for posts and rafters. Glulam is made from glued laminations, twists less and hardly splits. It is worth it mainly for beams with long spans. Larch and Douglas fir are naturally more weather resistant and can be used without chemical preservative.

Good detailing matters more than the species: never set posts into the ground. Stand them on post anchors clear of the ground, cover end grain and give the roof a generous overhang.

Snow load: why location matters

The snow load a roof has to carry depends on altitude and region. In upland areas and parts of Scotland it is much higher than in low-lying southern England. The “High snow load” option therefore chooses larger sections. It does not replace a structural calculation for your site.

Does a carport need planning permission?

It depends on where you live. In England and Wales many small outbuildings fall under permitted development, but there are limits on height, size and position, and an open carport attached to the house can be treated differently. Listed buildings, conservation areas and properties without permitted development rights have stricter rules. Scotland, Northern Ireland, Ireland and Australia have their own rules. Check with your local council before you build, or read the guidance on the Planning Portal.

Frequently asked questions

How far apart should carport rafters be?
For light roof coverings such as profiled metal sheets or polycarbonate, 600 to 900 mm centres are usual. The calculator spaces the rafters at about 700 mm. In the end, the roofing manufacturer's instructions decide.
What size posts does a carport need?
For single and double carports, 120 × 120 mm posts are common. With high snow load the calculator uses 140 × 140 mm. In the UK the nearest stock sizes are often 100 × 100, 125 × 125 or 150 × 150 mm, so choose the next size up.
How deep do the footings need to be?
Pad footings must be deep enough to sit below the frost line on firm ground. The right depth depends on the soil and region, so ask your local building control if you are unsure. Footings are not included in the calculator.
Does the calculator replace a structural engineer?
No. The sections are guide values for planning and buying timber. For safety, and where approval is needed, you need a structural calculation that takes snow, wind and the roof covering at your site into account.

All timber sections are guide values and do not replace a structural calculation. Carports and patio covers may need planning permission and building regulations approval, and a structural engineer's check depending on where you live.
